name: Exploring Canadian Geography
subject: Canadian and World Studies
description: This course builds on learning in Grades 7 and 8 in geography. Students will explore relationships within and between Canada’s natural and human systems and how they interconnect with other parts of the world. Students will also examine environmental and economic issues, and their impact related to topics such as natural resources and industries, careers, land use and responsible development, and sustainability. In addition, students will understand the connections that diverse communities and individuals have with the physical environment and each other throughout Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit perspectives. Students will apply geographic thinking, use the geographic inquiry process, and use geospatial technologies throughout their investigations.

specific_expectations.text: analyze how geological, hydrological, and climatic processes formed, and continue to shape, Canada’s landscape
specific_expectations.text_html: analyze how geological, hydrological, and climatic processes formed, and continue to shape, Canada’s landscape

elaborations.text:
Geological processes:

  plate tectonics caused, and continue to cause, folding and faulting in western Canada to create mountains and some active volcanoes
  ancient volcanism and more recent glacial erosion created the Canadian Shield
  continental glaciers sculpted and carved the Great Lakes basins, and localized glaciers continue to modify features in mountainous regions

Hydrological processes:

  flooding, tides, and wave action change coastlines, shorelines, and floodplains
  rivers and streams sculpt the landscape through erosion, transportation, and deposition, and these processes also help create new landforms
  sediments deposited at the bottom of an ancient inland sea eventually turned into bedrock and formed most of the landscape of today's Interior Plains 

Climatic processes:

  wind causes weathering and erosion in the badlands of Alberta
  proximity to large bodies of water impacts both temperature and precipitation

Hydrological processes:

Climatic processes:

  • proximity to large bodies of water impacts both temperature and precipitation

Consequences of changes:

  warming in the North is leading to a shorter, less reliable ice season, less snow cover, and changes in plant and animal populations (environmental); threatening traditional Inuit culture (social); expanding opportunities for resource exploitation (economic); and creating conflict between countries over territorial claims (political)
  melting of permafrost in Canada’s Arctic is leading to destabilization and shifting of buildings, including homes (social), and emissions of methane (environmental)
  increasing frequency and duration of drought on the Prairies reduces agricultural production (economic), which leads to higher grocery costs (social), and also impacts the health of ecosystems and plant and animal populations in the area, making them more susceptible to the spread of invasive species, disease, and population decline (environmental)

Mitigation and adaptation strategies:

  updating flood maps and local zoning by-laws to better prepare communities for the realities of flooding events made worse by climate change
  creating public spaces with less concrete and more greenery, such as by using porous paving and implementing urban greenery projects, to facilitate the absorption of water into soil and to cool down urban areas
  opening community cooling centres to serve unhoused people and those without air conditioning during heat warnings
  completing a carbon emissions audit for a new public building project and taking action to offset the project’s carbon footprint and mitigate its impact on climate change

  a region’s rock type determines which mineral resources are potentially available and the techniques used to extract and refine the minerals
  a region’s topography, precipitation, temperature, and soil type determine the type of agriculture that is practised there
  a region’s topography and hydrology determine the location of types of flow resources, such as wind and running/moving water, that can be used for electrical power generation
  the method for harvesting trees is determined by the forest type and physical geography of their location

  the development of wind turbine designs that are cold-weather friendly with de-icing and anti-icing mechanisms, which will allow turbines to continue operating efficiently under extreme conditions
  Canada’s invention and use of CANDU heavy water nuclear reactors, which can use natural (i.e., non-enriched) uranium as a fuel – a technology adopted by numerous countries worldwide in the effort to produce energy more sustainably
  the development of small modular reactors (SMRs), which are versatile and scalable and enable the building of nuclear infrastructure in a more cost-efficient way
  research and innovation around Ontario’s critical minerals, such as chromite, cobalt, nickel, copper, and platinum, in relation to future low- and zero-emission vehicles

  • What kinds of public services and infrastructure does a community need to remain socially stable and economically viable?
  • What are some grassroots strategies for social and economic sustainability being implemented by First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities?

  • What strategies are some local community groups in Canada implementing to increase the economic or social sustainability of their communities? How are these different from the strategies implemented by governments?
  • What economic criteria would a plan for improving environmental sustainability have to meet in order to be practical to adopt and viable in the long term?
  • What is the role of environmental stewardship in supporting a sustainable community?
